segment:
Mara watched, standing next to the two of them by the hallway doors, as he went back and picked up his empty glass and started in that direction, still chatting. He set the empty plastic glass down on a round table across from where she'd seen him leave the full one earlier. And walked away with Jonah.

She looked around again at the other people in the room. They were all either talking or making drinks. And it felt like they had all looked over at her now, and were waiting for her to speak up and join a conversation. But she still hadn't heard a word of what any of them were saying, because she was too busy watching for how the blond young man—Jonah—had just left his plastic glass on the wrong table, where she herself would be looking for a trash can.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

And that was when a door opened down the hallway behind her, releasing two voices into the room. One female, one male; one asking a question, the other replying; neither loud nor excited, just casual conversation. Jonah released her hand and turned away to look down the hall at them.
When Mara heard the voices and followed his gaze, she saw one young man who wasn’t Jonah, but close in size and shape; he had brown hair and a beard and was carrying a glass.

The brown-haired man glanced once over his shoulder, saw them standing there, nodded hello, and stepped right into the gathering, holding up his glass of wine—a half-full plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo on it. “Cheers.” He set it on the table against the wall to the left of the door, and stepped forward to shake Jonah’s hand as they exchanged names.

He set the empty plastic glass down on a round table across from where she'd seen him leave the full one earlier. And walked away with Jonah.

She looked around again at the other people in the room. They were all either talking or making drinks. And it felt like they had all looked over at her now, and were waiting for her to speak up and join a conversation. But she still hadn't heard a word of what any of them were saying, because she was too busy watching for how the blond young man—Jonah—had just left his plastic glass on the wrong table, where she herself would be looking for a trash can.

segment:
The brown-haired man glanced once over his shoulder, saw them standing there, nodded hello, and stepped right into the gathering, holding up his glass of wine—a half-full plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo on it. “Cheers.” He set it on the table against the wall to the left of the door, and stepped forward to shake Jonah’s hand as they exchanged names.

And when he turned away from that handshake, Mara noticed that his own face had darkened.
For one of his kind, he was tall. But his broad frame and soft brown eyes contrasted with the harshness around his mouth; his skin was dark, his hair black and close-cropped on the sides, and his beard thick but carefully trimmed. He was wearing a black T-shirt that covered up all of his arms but left most of his torso bare to show off a bit of flesh—and there it was, just barely visible above his collarbone: the tattoo.

“That’s Noah,” Jonah said as the brown-haired man stepped forward. “He’s been here a year.”

segment:
They had made some progress in talking before Mara saw the young fellow’s half-full cup of wine with the Fulcrum logo on it. She hadn't realized that the compound had a bar where drinks could be served, and she was vaguely aware that most people here avoided alcohol to ensure their alertness.

Then the fellow tossed it back in one gulp without setting it down, and said to Mara, "So how do you like the place?" And Mara felt her gut clench.

segment:
The brown-haired fellow didn’t release Jonah's hand even while talking to Mara: a quick handshake, a greeting, then a friendly nod, his gaze moving right on to take in Jonah from head to toe and then her again. Finally the other fellow dropped Jonah's hand and went back to his conversation.
Meanwhile, a woman in blue jeans and a blue Fulcrum T-shirt had set a plate on the counter in the kitchen and now stood behind the door in the entrance hall, not entering or leaving; she was turning back and forth, listening to the two fellows talk.

When she heard the next voice, a female voice from the direction of her office, Mara turned and smiled at her new visitor. But as her glance went back toward the kitchen, something struck her. The woman in the Fulcrum T-shirt had picked up Jonah's half-full cup and moved it off to one side while carrying on her conversation with the other fellow. He still didn't notice what she was doing.

segment:
And now that they were both turned sideways, Mara saw two others coming into the room from behind her: a pair of adults who looked like friends or family. She still had to find the people she'd come here to interview.

The newcomer nodded to Jonah and to his brown-haired friend in passing, heading for a low table on the other side of the room.
Mara noticed that his clothing was darker than the blond man's: a gray T-shirt and darker shorts, bare legs again but a little longer, and he moved with the long confident stride of someone who had done this many times before, going straight to a spot at the back of the room where he could lean against the padded wall with his elbows bent. His wife followed behind him and gave everyone a friendly smile, looking like someone's mother but younger, in a green T-shirt and shorts.

segment:
The third man turned to Mara, held out his hand, and smiled.
“I’m Andrew.”
When the young woman spoke up, Mara didn’t expect that. They could have introduced each other; she could have waited her turn, even stayed silent. But she didn’t.

“Mara!” The girl came into the room then, in a full-length black dress that flared out at her ankles and a shawl covering her head in long triangular folds, walking straight toward Mara with her arms wide and ready. When Mara held out her own, the girl threw her arms around her shoulders and hugged, holding on for several full seconds before pulling away with a smile.

“Hi!”
And then she reached out to shake hands, too, and said her name.
“Amelia.”
